questions: A logical partition of a cluster that scopes names, RBAC, quotas and policies for a group of resources
Namespaces (projects in OpenShift) group and isolate resources logically, acting as the boundary for RBAC, ResourceQuota and NetworkPolicy.
cp4i-dev, cp4i-test and cp4i-prod are namespaces with different access rules.
Namespace = the unit of tenancy in Kubernetes.

An enterprise wants to run CP4I on OpenShift in both an on-premises data center and a public cloud, with consistent governance and fleet management of the clusters. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

Use a multi-cluster management layer (for example Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management) with GitOps (Argo CD ApplicationSets) to apply consistent policies, operator versions and CP4I configuration to each cluster, while capability-level replication handles data where required
Manage each cluster manually with different procedures
Stretch a single cluster between the data center and the cloud
Run CP4I only in the cloud and connect on-premises systems through public internet APIs
Fleet management plus GitOps provides consistent configuration, policy compliance and visibility across hybrid clusters. Data replication remains capability-specific.
Wrong: ignores hybrid requirements and security.
ACM policies enforce cert-manager and NetworkPolicy baselines; an ApplicationSet deploys the same CP4I operator versions to all clusters.
Hybrid multi-cluster = central policy + GitOps + per-capability replication.
After a node pool upgrade, all three Event Streams brokers ended up on two nodes in the same zone, although preferred anti-affinity was configured. Why could this happen, and how can it be prevented?

Preferred (soft) anti-affinity is best-effort; during constrained rescheduling the scheduler may co-locate pods. Use required anti-affinity or topologySpreadConstraints with whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule on the zone key, and keep capacity in every zone
Anti-affinity does not work for StatefulSets
Zones are not supported by Kafka
Soft rules can be violated when capacity is tight. Hard constraints guarantee spreading, but require enough capacity per zone, or pods stay Pending.
Correct: soft versus hard constraints, plus capacity.
topologySpreadConstraints with maxSkew 1 on topology.kubernetes.io/zone and DoNotSchedule keeps brokers spread.
Soft rules bend; hard rules block. Choose based on the cost of co-location.
An operator upgrade InstallPlan fails because a new CRD version removes a field still used by existing custom resources stored in etcd. What does this indicate, and what should the team do?

The upgrade path skipped a required intermediate version or migration step (storage version migration); follow the documented upgrade path through the supported operator versions and verify CR compatibility before upgrading
Delete all existing CRs to let the upgrade proceed
Force-install the operator ignoring the error
CRD schema changes need supported upgrade paths that migrate stored objects. Skipping versions or forcing upgrades risks data loss.
Correct: follow the supported upgrade path and migration.
The team upgrades through the intermediate channel first, as the release notes require.
Respect supported upgrade paths; CRD versions matter.

A company must expose Event Streams, MQ and APIs from one OpenShift cluster to partners on dedicated public IPs, separate from employee-facing applications, with independent scaling. What design is MOST appropriate?

Create a dedicated IngressController (router shard) published by a separate load balancer or IP for partner traffic, select partner routes by label or namespace, run it on dedicated infra nodes, and use passthrough routes for TLS-native protocols (MQ, Kafka) with SNI
Use NodePort services on every worker
Expose everything through the default router
Give partners VPN access to the pod network
Router sharding gives traffic isolation, dedicated IPs and independent scaling. Passthrough with SNI supports MQ and Kafka TLS traffic.
Correct: a dedicated partner ingress shard.
Wrong: a large attack surface and hard to manage.
The partner-ingress controller runs on two infra nodes in the DMZ VLAN with its own load balancer IP.
What happens when a container tries to use more memory than its memory limit?
The container is terminated (OOMKilled) and restarted according to the pod's restart policy
Memory is not compressible. Exceeding the limit causes the kernel OOM killer to terminate the container. CPU, by contrast, is throttled.
An ACE container limited to 1Gi is OOMKilled when a 900 MB file is parsed in memory.
Memory limit hit = kill. CPU limit hit = throttle.
